prompt: Drag through what happens to retention of something you learned today, with one well-timed review along the way:

steps.label: Right after learning it
steps.content: Retention is near its peak - you can recall it easily. This is also the point where it feels safest to assume it's "learned" and move on, which is exactly the trap: this feeling doesn't predict how much will still be there in a few days.

steps.label: 1 day later, no review
steps.content: A significant chunk is already gone - this is the steepest part of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve. Not because anything went wrong; this is the default trajectory for anything encountered once and never revisited.

steps.label: 1 week later, no review
steps.content: Most of what wasn't reinforced has faded well below what's practically usable. This is roughly where a lot of "I learned this once" knowledge quietly ends up - technically encountered, functionally gone.

steps.label: The intervention: one quick review, timed right
steps.content: A short retrieval-practice check right around the point retention was about to drop off - not a full re-read, just actively trying to recall it - resets the curve. Critically, the NEW curve after this review decays more slowly than the first one did.

steps.label: After a second well-timed review
steps.content: Each subsequent review flattens the curve further, and the gap before the next necessary review gets longer. This is the actual mechanism behind spaced-repetition systems: not reviewing more, but reviewing at the specific point it's about to be needed, and letting that point drift later each time.
